turn_text: Well, there's a lot of work that we need to do as Democrats, you know, and I know very well that your listenership is, they're Democrats listening to this and Republicans and independents, people who don't identify with any party, but I think that when it all is said and done, we're human beings, and when we elect people to represent us, whether it be in our state houses or in Washington, D.C., they want to make sure that we're listening to them. And as a result of listening to them that we write and pass legislation that is reflective of what needs to be done. So in this role that I have, I'm the only Midwesterner sitting around the Democratic House leadership, elected leadership in Washington. And I mean, I think we come to our decisions based on what exactly what I just said. You know, we know that We were put on this earth with two ears and one mouth and I think we were designed to use those proportionately and that's what I try to do. What I'm working on now is talking with not just my colleagues but people who are running for Congress in various offices about making sure that we don't just show up in towns of 50,000 or more but we go to towns that might just have 100 or 200 people and we listen to them. And the way I do that specifically is I do a couple things. That can be certainly no, you know, science-based approach to it by any means, but on Saturdays, we do something that we call supermarket Saturday. Just walk up and down the aisles of the grocery store and talk to people. You know, if they're not rushing through with their cart and need to get home to their kids or to a ballgame, you know, we stop them in the cornflake aisle and we just say, you know, what do you want me to know before I fly back out to Washington? And, you know, it's unscripted. It's just top of mind for people. And we use that to figure out what we're going to be focusing on out here in Washington. And one other thing I do is we call it Sherry on Shift, which is nothing more than me job shadowing people. And standing shoulder to shoulder, whether it be with a welder, a car repairman, a forklift driver, a carp processor, UPS driver, whatever it is. And we have a nice conversation about how they're supporting their families, their challenges, whether they were able to buy a new pickup truck in the last 10 years, whether they were able to take their families on vacation. And what we do know is that before the Affordable Care Act passed that we as a nation were on an unsustainable path in our health care delivery system, the cost for rising at double-digit rates year after year, We had record numbers of bankruptcies that were being filed by families who couldn't afford to pay their health care bills. We had people who were knocked off their insurance once they would hit their cap. We had people with preexisting conditions who couldn't even get health care insurance. We had too many people getting their primary care out of emergency rooms, which is the most expensive way to deliver health care. And on top of it, we had 50 million uninsured Americans at that time. So the fact that the Congress undertook reforming healthcare was an exercise worth going through and the passage of the Affordable Care Act while a flawed bill was at least a step in the right direction. And I don't have to go through the litany of things that people like because I think it's clear that when your kid who is working in a company doesn't have health insurance and can stay on your parents health care, up to age 26, that was pretty good. And when we could get preventive care at no cost, which was in the end of savings to the health care system, all that's good. However, the cost of health care is still too high. And the answer is not passing this bill that actually did pass the House and had it not been for John McCain would have passed the Senate. It was a terrible approach. Because we would go back to the days where we would have, at that, as a result of those pieces of legislation, we would have had more than 20 million people knocked off their healthcare. In my state of Illinois, we would have lost 65,000 healthcare jobs, and you can multiply that by states all over the country. There would be about 700 rural hospitals that would have closed. And not to mention that the, you know, people with pre-existing conditions just not knowing where to turn because healthcare would have been so unaffordable.
